Origin: /claude-tweaks:feedback session-evaluation (self-assessment, degraded from a failed Frontier judge dispatch), self-referential run (this repo's own origin is thomasholknielsen/claude-tweaks) — routed to a normal backlog record per Step 3 rather than filed as upstream feedback.

## Current State

`node plugin/bin/release.js <minor|patch> "<summary>" --dry-run` (and the live invocation) emits roughly 490 lines of `fatal: path '<path>' exists on disk, but not in '<sha>'` git stderr noise while walking history to locate the last version-bump commit, before reaching its actual result. In one observed run, 492 of 497 total output lines were this noise; only the final ~5 lines (`[dry-run] would bump ...`) were the actual answer, forcing the output to be redirected to a file and tailed rather than read directly.

## Deliverables

Either suppress/redirect the walk's expected-to-fail probe commands' stderr internally in `plugin/bin/lib/release/` (the history-walk implementation), or stop the walk as soon as a version-bump commit is found rather than continuing all the way to the repo root.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `node plugin/bin/release.js <minor|patch> "<summary>" --dry-run` produces output whose vast majority is the actual result (the bump preview lines), with no `fatal: ...` git stderr noise reaching stdout/stderr for commits before the file existed at its current path.

Origin: /claude-tweaks:feedback session-evaluation (self-assessment, degraded from a failed Frontier judge dispatch), self-referential run (this repo's own origin is thomasholknielsen/claude-tweaks) — routed to a normal backlog record per Step 3 rather than filed as upstream feedback.

## Current State

Worktrees created via the harness-native `EnterWorktree` tool (rather than `plugin/skills/dispatch/`'s own `record-worktree` CLI) never get their worktree/branch association written into that run's `run-state.json`. Downstream, `teardown-run`/`archive-run` (`plugin/bin/hooks.js`) can't find the association and report "no worktree recorded" instead of tearing the worktree down automatically. In one session this recurred across 7 separate worktrees, each requiring a manual `git merge-base --is-ancestor` proof + `git worktree remove --force` + `git branch -D` + `gh api -X DELETE .../refs/heads/{branch}` sequence in place of one CLI call — roughly 14 extra manual commands that a working association would have made unnecessary. A related recovery-quality symptom from the same gap: a prior session's main checkout was found 256 commits behind `origin/main` while still holding uncommitted archival bookkeeping from an earlier `/tidy` run — state left behind with no automatic reconciliation path, blocking a later session's own `archive-run` calls until manually resolved via a scratch-worktree PR.

Related, narrower observation from the same evaluation: the ledger's canonical Create location (`docs/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-{feature}-ledger.md`, per `_shared/ledger-format.md`) requires a worktree write under `worktree-always`, but `residue-sweep.md` explicitly expects a standalone (no-worktree) wrap-up run to be able to create one "so the ledger's own resolve gate has something to enforce on a standalone run." In practice a standalone run has no lightweight path to satisfy this — creating a ledger file for a single non-blocking item means a full worktree-commit-push-PR-merge cycle for a file that gets deleted moments later once resolved.

## Deliverables

1. Either make `EnterWorktree` call `record-worktree` itself when the harness detects a claude-tweaks-managed repo, or make `teardown-run`/`archive-run` fall back to `git worktree list`/branch-name matching when `run-state.json` carries no worktree field.
2. Let a standalone, no-worktree wrap-up log ledger items to a location that doesn't require a worktree write — e.g. `.claude-tweaks/pipelines/{run-id}/` (already commit-exempt under `worktree-always` and already the run's own audit-trail home) instead of `docs/plans/`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A worktree entered via `EnterWorktree` during a dispatch/wrap-up run is torn down by `teardown-run`/`archive-run` without a "no worktree recorded" failure and without any manual `git worktree remove`/`git branch -D`/`gh api DELETE` fallback.
- A standalone wrap-up run with at least one ledger item can create, resolve, and delete its ledger without needing a worktree, a commit, or a PR.

groups.body:
Surface: infra

## Current State

`_shared/worktree-setup.md`'s "Adopt-or-create" gate (confirmed, ~lines 29-65) has an "Already
isolated" (adopt) branch that runs a clean-tree precondition check and a
fetch+merge-against-origin catch-up, but nowhere checks whether the adopted worktree's own
`node_modules` matches its own `package.json`/lockfile — confirmed by grep: zero mentions of
`node_modules`, `npm install`, or `npm ci` anywhere in either `_shared/worktree-setup.md` or
`build/worktree-setup.md`. When the worktree has no local `node_modules` at all, Node's module
resolution walks up to the main checkout's copy, which can be stale relative to the worktree's
own branch (e.g. missing a dependency the branch just added). The result is cascading
`ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` failures across every test that imports the missing dependency — a
misleading, unrelated-looking symptom that costs real investigation time before the actual cause
is found.

Observed live: in a Next.js/TypeScript project, an adopted worktree had no local `node_modules`,
so Node resolved to the main checkout's copy, which predated two dependencies (`unified`,
`remark-parse`) the worktree's own branch had already added. The pre-flight test sweep failed
near-total, unrelated to any actual code change. The fix was running `npm ci` plus a
client-generation step inside the worktree itself.

**Scope note for the builder:** neither worktree-setup file mentions a dependency-install step at
all, for either the adopt path or the fresh-creation path — verify at build time whether a fresh
`EnterWorktree`-created worktree already gets `node_modules` some other way (a symlink, a
documented install step living elsewhere in `build/SKILL.md` or `flow/SKILL.md` rather than in
the worktree-setup files themselves) before assuming this gap is adopted-worktree-specific; if
fresh creation has the identical exposure, the fix belongs in the shared gate both paths already
route through, not only the adopt branch.

## Deliverables

Add a detection-and-message (or auto-install) step to the Adopt-or-create gate's adopt branch:
when the worktree has no local `node_modules` (or one that's stale relative to
`package.json`/the lockfile), either run the install automatically or surface a clear message
naming the mismatch before the caller proceeds to run tests — so a missing/stale dependency
produces an actionable message immediately, not a cascade of misleading
`ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` failures deep into a test run.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Adopting a worktree with no local `node_modules` produces either an automatic install or a
  clear, actionable message before any test/build step runs — not a silent walk-up resolution to
  the main checkout's (potentially stale) copy.
- The check/fix correctly distinguishes "no local `node_modules` at all" from "local
  `node_modules` present and current" — an already-correct worktree pays no extra cost.
- `npm test` passes.

## Technical Approach

Add a check to the Adopt-or-create gate's adopt branch (~line 49, in the same sequence as the
existing clean-tree precondition check and fetch+merge catch-up): test for the presence of a
local `node_modules` directory in the worktree root, and — if missing, or if a cheap staleness
signal is available (e.g. comparing `package-lock.json`'s mtime/hash against a stamp
`node_modules` itself carries, if this project's package manager writes one) — either run the
project's own install command (detected the same way `dev-url-detection.md` already detects a
project's dev/start command, per this codebase's existing conventions for that kind of
detection) or emit a clear warning naming the gap and recommending `npm ci` (or the detected
package manager's equivalent) before proceeding. Prefer surfacing a clear message over a silent
auto-install if there's any ambiguity about which package manager or install command applies —
a wrong auto-install could itself cost more time than the original failure mode.

### Key Files

- `plugin/skills/_shared/worktree-setup.md` — add the check to the Adopt-or-create gate's adopt
  branch (~line 49)
- `plugin/skills/build/worktree-setup.md` — verify whether the fresh-creation path also needs
  this check, per the Current State's scope note

## Gotchas

- Don't assume a specific package manager (npm/pnpm/yarn) — detect it the way this codebase
  already detects other project-specific commands (lockfile presence is usually the simplest
  signal: `package-lock.json` → npm, `pnpm-lock.yaml` → pnpm, `yarn.lock` → yarn).
- An auto-install can be slow (real dependency resolution) — if choosing auto-install over a
  message-only approach, make sure it doesn't silently add significant wall-clock time to every
  worktree adoption without at least logging that it's happening.
- Per the Current State's scope note: confirm whether this is genuinely adopted-worktree-specific
  before landing a fix only in the adopt branch — a fresh-creation gap in the same class would be
  a bigger miss to leave unaddressed.

## Original request

**Summary:** An adopted (already-isolated) worktree with no local `node_modules` silently resolves dependencies via Node's parent-directory walk-up to the main checkout's copy, which can predate what the worktree's own branch declares in `package.json`.

**Kind:** Gap

**Affected component:** `build/worktree-setup.md`'s Adopt-or-create gate (and/or the pre-flight verify sweep)

**Use case:** Running `/claude-tweaks:build` or `/claude-tweaks:flow` against a worktree that was adopted rather than freshly created by `EnterWorktree` -- the gate only checks that the worktree is isolated and clean, not that its own `node_modules` matches its own `package.json`/lockfile. When the worktree has no local `node_modules` at all, Node's module resolution walks up to the main checkout's copy, which can be stale relative to the worktree's own branch (e.g. missing a dependency the branch just added). The result is cascading `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` failures across every test that imports the missing dependency -- a misleading, unrelated-looking symptom that costs real investigation time before the actual cause is found.

Observed live: in a Next.js/TypeScript project (a private project), an adopted worktree had no local `node_modules`, so Node resolved to the main checkout's copy, which predated two dependencies (`unified`, `remark-parse`) the worktree's own branch had already added. The pre-flight test sweep failed near-total, unrelated to any actual code change. The fix was running `npm ci` plus a client-generation step inside the worktree itself.

**Definition:** Clear -- the fix is a single, well-scoped detection-and-message (or auto-install) step; there's no genuine open tradeoff to specify further.

**Plugin version:** 6.114.1

Surface: infra

**Related:** #1728, #1734, #1738, #1811, #1826, #1841, #1892, #1982, #2032, #2051, #2081, #2226, #2228, #2229, #2230, #2231, #2240, #2330, #2332 (near-duplicate screen hits — shared file-path/anchor mentions only, not confirmed duplicates of this record's own topic)

## Current State

In one seven-spec multi-record run, eight commits failed with
`fatal: Unable to create '<repo>/.git/index.lock': File exists`. The lock holder was a sibling
agent's git call or a PostToolUse hook in the same checkout, never a stale process — every one of
them succeeded on a retry a couple of seconds later. The run only got through because the ad-hoc
ledger-append scripts written for it grew their own 2-second retry loop; nothing in the plugin
provided one.

The plugin's own commit call sites run `git commit` through `execFileSync` with no retry at all:

- `bin/lib/reconcile/archive-merged.js` — `runGit(['commit', '-m', '[reconcile] archive run …'])`
- `bin/lib/release/run.js` — `deps.git(['commit', '-m', 'Release v… — …'])`
- `bin/release-local.js` — `deps.git(['commit', '-m', 'chore(release): v…'])`

A transient index-lock collision at any of these surfaces as a hard failure of a reconcile or
release step, in exactly the multi-agent setting the plugin is built for (parallel dispatch,
worktrees, hooks running git in the background). The sanctioned run-dir writers
(`log-decision.js`, `stage-item.js`, `set-config.js`) never take the index lock and are unaffected;
`bin/lib/file-lock.js` is a directory mutex for file stores, not git's index.

The precedent for the exact shape already exists one directory over:
`bin/lib/feedback/file-feedback.js`'s `withTransientRetry(runner, { waitMs, maxRetries, sleep })`
(confirmed, line 70) wraps `gh` calls on a transient-error signature, with an injectable `sleep` so
tests do not wait. Nothing equivalent guards git. A standing memory entry already records the
operator-side rule for this failure ("retry, never `rm` the lock"); the plugin's own code does not
follow it.

## Deliverables

- A shared bounded retry for index-lock contention — `bin/lib/git-retry.js` exporting
  `withIndexLockRetry(gitRunner, { attempts, waitMs, sleep })`, shaped like
  `withTransientRetry`: retry **only** on a stderr signature naming `index.lock`
  (`Unable to create … index.lock` / `another git process seems to be running`), bounded
  (~15 attempts at 2 s), injectable `sleep`, and never unlinking a lock file.
- Route every plugin commit call site through it: `bin/lib/reconcile/archive-merged.js`,
  `bin/lib/release/run.js`, `bin/release-local.js`.
- State the rule once where skill prose instructs a commit, so a hand-written commit path
  retries the same way instead of each script growing its own loop, and cite it rather than
  restating it (CLAUDE.md's cross-reference rule).

## Acceptance Criteria

1. `withIndexLockRetry` retries on an `index.lock` stderr signature and does **not** retry on any
   other git failure — both directions asserted with a fake runner (a fake failing on
   `index.lock` twice then succeeding produces one commit and no error; a fake failing on an
   unrelated git error fails on the first attempt).
2. The helper never unlinks a lock file — asserted directly, not merely absent from the source.
3. Retries are bounded: a fake runner that always fails on `index.lock` exits after the configured
   attempt count with the original git error, and the injected `sleep` makes the test instant.
4. Each of the three named commit call sites routes through the helper (grep proves no direct
   `['commit', …]` call bypasses it), and `npm test` passes.

## Non-Goals

- Replacing the sanctioned run-dir writers' `file-lock.js` mutex; it guards a different resource.
- Any change to what the commits contain or when they run — only how a transient lock is survived.

## Technical Approach

Model `bin/lib/git-retry.js`'s `withIndexLockRetry` directly on the existing
`withTransientRetry` pattern in `bin/lib/feedback/file-feedback.js:70` — same shape (a wrapping
higher-order function taking a runner and an options object with an injectable `sleep`), but
keyed on a different error signature: match stderr for `index.lock` or `another git process seems
to be running` rather than `file-feedback.js`'s own transient-`gh`-error signature. Wrap each of
the three named call sites' `git(['commit', ...])` invocation with it, passing each site's
existing runner through unchanged — this is a call-site wrapping, not a rewrite of any of the
three modules' own commit logic. Then find wherever skill prose (a `SKILL.md` or `_shared/*.md`
file) instructs an agent to run `git commit` directly as part of a documented procedure, and add
one citation to this new shared retry rule there (per this codebase's cross-reference convention:
state the rule once, cite it everywhere) rather than restating the retry logic in prose at each
site.

### Key Files

- `plugin/bin/lib/git-retry.js` — new file, `withIndexLockRetry` (model on
  `bin/lib/feedback/file-feedback.js`'s `withTransientRetry`)
- `plugin/bin/lib/reconcile/archive-merged.js` — route its `commit` call through the new retry
- `plugin/bin/lib/release/run.js` — route its `commit` call through the new retry
- `plugin/bin/release-local.js` — route its `commit` call through the new retry
- A skill/`_shared/*.md` file instructing a hand-written `git commit` in prose — add one citation
  to the new rule (exact file identified via a grep at build time)

## Gotchas

- Never unlink the lock file — this is an explicit, tested requirement (Acceptance Criterion 2),
  not an incidental detail; a standing memory entry in this repo records this as the
  operator-side rule the plugin's own code is catching up to.
- Match the retry signature narrowly (`index.lock` / "another git process seems to be running")
  — a broad transient-error match would risk silently retrying a genuine, non-lock git failure
  and masking it behind a multi-attempt delay.
- The sanctioned run-dir writers (`log-decision.js`, `stage-item.js`, `set-config.js`) are
  explicitly out of scope — they use a different lock mechanism (`file-lock.js`, a directory
  mutex) for a different resource, and don't take git's index lock at all.

## Original request

groups.body:
Surface: infra

## Current State

Found during a pre-release whole-branch review of `plugin/bin/lib/reconcile/archive-merged.js`.
New failure reasons `work-twin-conflict` (confirmed, ~line 684) and
`work-twin-resolve-failed[-partial-revert]` are never tracked toward residue escalation, so a
genuinely diverged work twin is skipped silently on every reconcile pass forever — no streak, no
issue filed.

`trackArchiveResult` (confirmed, ~line 1083) early-returns `if (result.reason !== 'move-failed')
return;` before reaching `trackResidue`, and `STRUCTURALLY_STUCK_REASONS` (confirmed, line 1030)
is `new Set(['no-worktree', 'no-branch', 'no-pr'])` — it doesn't include either new twin reason.

## Deliverables

Extend `trackArchiveResult`/`STRUCTURALLY_STUCK_REASONS` (or add an equivalent path) so a
`work-twin-conflict`/`work-twin-resolve-failed[-partial-revert]` result accumulates toward the
same residue-escalation streak as the existing structurally-stuck reasons, rather than being
silently dropped every pass.

## Acceptance Criteria

A reconcile run that repeatedly hits `work-twin-conflict` on the same run dir eventually
escalates (streak-based issue filing), the same way a repeated `no-worktree`/`no-branch`/`no-pr`
result does today.

## Technical Approach

Widen `trackArchiveResult`'s early-return guard (~line 1083) from the single literal
`result.reason !== 'move-failed'` to also accept `work-twin-conflict` and
`work-twin-resolve-failed`/`work-twin-resolve-failed-partial-revert`, routing them into the same
`trackResidue(root, repoSlug, {reason}, dir, { failed: true, lastError: result.lastError },
{ escalate })` call the `move-failed` path already uses — reuse the existing choke point rather
than duplicating escalation logic. Decide whether the twin reasons need their own `reason` key
passed to `trackResidue` (distinct from `'move-failed'`) so `escalate-residue.js`'s filed-issue
title/body correctly names "work-twin-conflict" rather than generically reusing "move-failed" —
this affects how a human reading the escalated issue understands what actually went wrong, so
prefer the more specific reason string.

### Key Files

- `plugin/bin/lib/reconcile/archive-merged.js` — widen `trackArchiveResult`'s reason guard
  (~line 1083) to also route `work-twin-conflict`/`work-twin-resolve-failed[-partial-revert]`
  into `trackResidue`

## Gotchas

- `STRUCTURALLY_STUCK_REASONS` (line 1030) governs a *different* mechanism (the
  `isStructurallyStuck()`/`no-branch`-class TTL-based staleness check) than
  `trackArchiveResult`'s own `move-failed`-keyed residue tracking — don't conflate the two; this
  record's fix is about routing the twin reasons into `trackResidue`'s escalation streak, not
  necessarily adding them to `STRUCTURALLY_STUCK_REASONS` itself (which governs a specific,
  separate no-worktree/no-branch/no-pr classification). Verify which mechanism actually needs
  the new reasons before changing both.
- A `work-twin-resolve-failed-partial-revert` is a worse state than a clean `work-twin-conflict`
  (a partially-applied revert) — make sure the escalated issue's body can distinguish the two
  reasons, not just lump them under one generic label, since a human resolving the escalation
  needs to know which situation they're looking at.

## Original request

## Current State
Found during a pre-release whole-branch review of `plugin/bin/lib/reconcile/archive-merged.js`. New failure reasons `work-twin-conflict` and `work-twin-resolve-failed[-partial-revert]` (~line 684) are never tracked toward residue escalation, so a genuinely diverged work twin is skipped silently on every reconcile pass forever — no streak, no issue filed.

`trackArchiveResult` (~line 1076) early-returns `if (result.reason !== 'move-failed') return;` before reaching `trackResidue`, and `STRUCTURALLY_STUCK_REASONS` (~line 1023) is `{'no-worktree','no-branch','no-pr'}` — it doesn't include either new twin reason.

## Deliverables
Extend `trackArchiveResult`/`STRUCTURALLY_STUCK_REASONS` (or add an equivalent path) so a `work-twin-conflict`/`work-twin-resolve-failed[-partial-revert]` result accumulates toward the same residue-escalation streak as the existing structurally-stuck reasons, rather than being silently dropped every pass.

## Acceptance Criteria
A reconcile run that repeatedly hits `work-twin-conflict` on the same run dir eventually escalates (streak-based issue filing), the same way a repeated `no-worktree`/`no-branch`/`no-pr` result does today.

Surface: infra

## Current State

`bin/verify.js` (the shared `/claude-tweaks:test` and `/claude-tweaks:build` verification
runner) reserves only one `"types"` check name for the fail-fast-before-tests tier, alongside
`"lint"` — confirmed by grep: the literal strings `'types'`/`'lint'` are hardcoded at multiple
points (`verify.js:212`'s `allowed` set, `:265`'s static-check branch, `:281`'s `staticNames`
filter, `:387` and `:451`'s `suitesRun` filters). A monorepo can have multiple independent
typecheck commands with no way to give more than one that treatment.

A pnpm/npm workspace monorepo with multiple independently-typed packages (e.g. three packages
each needing their own `tsc --noEmit`, with no single command that covers all three) wants
typecheck and lint to run independently of whether `tests` happens to pass. Naming the extra
typecheck commands something else (e.g. `types-core`, `types-worker`, `types-web`) demotes them
to the "any other name" tier, which runs serially **after** `tests` succeeds under the same
fail-fast policy — so when `tests` fails for a reason unrelated to any of the typechecks (e.g. a
flaky test-hook timeout under concurrent machine load), all three typechecks get skipped
(`skipped: fail-fast`) even though none of them actually depend on `tests` passing. A caller then
has to notice the `skipped: fail-fast` rows and re-run each typecheck command by hand, outside
the runner, to get a real signal.

Reproduction: `node bin/verify.js --cmd types-core="..." --cmd types-worker="..." --cmd
types-web="..." --cmd lint="..." --cmd tests="..."` where `tests` fails for any reason —
`report.json` shows `types-core`/`types-worker`/`types-web` as `{"skipped": "fail-fast"}` even
though each is independent of `tests`.

## Deliverables

Choose and implement one of:

- **(a) Widen the reserved tier**: let multiple checks share the reserved pre-`tests` tier — e.g.
  any `--cmd` name prefixed `types:` or `types-` joins the same concurrent-with-lint,
  fail-fast-before-tests group the single `types` name gets today. This requires updating every
  hardcoded `'types'`/`'lint'` comparison site (`verify.js:212`, `:265`, `:281`, `:387`, `:451`)
  to a prefix-match instead of an exact-string match.
- **(b) Document the workaround**: explicitly document that a monorepo with N independent
  typecheck commands should invoke them as their own `verify.js` call, or combine them into one
  compound `--cmd types="a && b && c"`, rather than as N separately-named checks — so the
  fail-fast-skip behavior is expected rather than surprising.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Whichever option is chosen, a monorepo with multiple independent typecheck commands has a
  documented, working path to get fail-fast-before-tests treatment for all of them (not just one
  named `types`) — either because the runner now supports it natively (option a), or because the
  documented workaround (a compound `--cmd` or multiple `verify.js` invocations) is proven to
  work and is referenced from `bin/verify.js`'s own usage/help text or its skill documentation.
- If option (a): every one of the five hardcoded `'types'`/`'lint'` comparison sites is updated
  consistently — a partial update (e.g. widening the `allowed` set at line 212 but not the
  `suitesRun` filters at 387/451) would produce an inconsistent runner.
- `npm test` passes.

## Technical Approach

Read all five call sites (`verify.js:212, 265, 281, 387, 451`) together before choosing an
approach — they must all agree on what counts as a "types-tier" check name, or the runner's
own internal bookkeeping (`suitesRun`, `staticNames`, the `allowed` set) will disagree with each
other. If choosing (a), define the widened match once (a shared predicate or regex, e.g.
`/^types(-|$)/`) and use it at every site rather than duplicating the pattern five times. If
choosing (b), the fix is documentation-only — add the guidance to `bin/verify.js`'s own
`--help`/usage text and to whichever skill file documents its `--cmd` naming convention for
callers.

### Key Files

- `plugin/bin/verify.js` (lines 212, 265, 281, 387, 451) — the five call sites that would need a
  consistent widened match under option (a)
- Skill documentation for `/claude-tweaks:test` / `/claude-tweaks:build`'s verify.js invocation
  convention — where option (b)'s guidance would live, or where option (a)'s new naming
  convention would need documenting either way

## Gotchas

- This is a genuine design choice between (a) runner capability vs. (b) documented workaround —
  the record's own Deliverables frame both as valid; don't treat one as obviously correct without
  weighing the blast radius of changing shared verification-runner logic (option a) against the
  lower-risk, purely-documentary option (b).
- If choosing (a), verify the widened match doesn't accidentally capture an unrelated check name
  a caller might legitimately want in the post-tests tier (e.g. a check literally named
  `types-of-fun` that has nothing to do with typechecking) — a prefix match on `types-`/`types:`
  is a judgment call about false-positive risk, not a free lunch.

## Original request

**Summary:** bin/verify.js reserves only one "types" check name for the fail-fast-before-tests tier, but a monorepo can have multiple independent typecheck commands with no way to give more than one that treatment.

**Kind:** Gap

**Affected component:** bin/verify.js (the shared /claude-tweaks:test and /claude-tweaks:build verification runner)

**Use case:** A pnpm/npm workspace monorepo with multiple independently-typed packages (e.g. three packages each needing their own `tsc --noEmit`, with no single command that covers all three) wants typecheck and lint to run independently of whether `tests` happens to pass. verify.js's ordering policy treats exactly one `--cmd` name, `types`, as reserved for the "run before tests, fail-fast on failure" tier, alongside `lint`. Naming the extra typecheck commands something else (e.g. `types-core`, `types-worker`, `types-web`) demotes them to the "any other name" tier, which runs serially **after** `tests` succeeds under the same fail-fast policy — so when `tests` fails for a reason unrelated to any of the typechecks (e.g. a flaky test-hook timeout under concurrent machine load), all three typechecks get skipped (`skipped: fail-fast`) even though none of them actually depend on `tests` passing. A caller then has to notice the `skipped: fail-fast` rows and re-run each typecheck command by hand, outside the runner, to get a real signal.

**Suggested fix:** either (a) let multiple checks share the reserved pre-`tests` tier — e.g. any `--cmd` name prefixed `types:` or `types-` joins the same concurrent-with-lint, fail-fast-before-tests group the single `types` name gets today — or (b) document explicitly that a monorepo with N independent typecheck commands should invoke them as their own verify.js call (or combine them into one compound `--cmd types="a && b && c"`) rather than as N separately-named checks, so the fail-fast-skip behavior is expected rather than surprising.

**Reproduction:** `node bin/verify.js --cmd types-core="..." --cmd types-worker="..." --cmd types-web="..." --cmd lint="..." --cmd tests="..."` where `tests` fails for any reason — `report.json` shows `types-core`/`types-worker`/`types-web` as `{"skipped": "fail-fast"}` even though each is independent of `tests`.

**Definition:** Clear

**Plugin version:** 6.118.0

Surface: infra

## Current State

Found during a pre-release whole-branch review. Migrating `plugin/bin/lib/verify/stamp.js` off
the deleted `writeJsonAtomic` silently changed the temp filename shape from `${jsonPath}.tmp` to
`${basename}.tmp-${pid}` (confirmed, ~line 63: `writeFileAtomic(jsonPath, ...)`): the old
`lib/verify/atomic-write.js` used `const tmpPath = \`${filePath}.tmp\`;` while the replacement
(confirmed, `lib/atomic-write.js:27`) uses `path.join(dir, \`${path.basename(filePath)}.tmp-${process.pid}\`)`.
Any fixture, cleanup script, or `.gitignore` entry keyed on the old literal no longer matches.

Separately, `tests/bin-lib/verify/stamp.test.js:60`'s new pid-suffix pin covers only the
verify-pass stamp write; the count-stamp write migrated in the same commit (confirmed,
`verify.js:374`: `writeFileAtomic(countStampPath, ...)`) is unpinned. The deleted
`tests/bin-lib/verify/atomic-write.test.js` was the only place that had covered the count-stamp
write shape, and nothing replaced that coverage. The legacy bare-SHA twin write two lines below
the count-stamp call (confirmed, `stamp.js:69`: `const tmp = \`${legacyPath}.tmp\`;`) still uses
the old `.tmp` shape, unmigrated.

## Deliverables

- Sweep for any remaining references to the old `.tmp` (no pid suffix) filename shape.
- Add a test pinning the count-stamp write's temp-filename shape, matching the coverage the
  deleted `atomic-write.test.js` used to provide.
- Confirm the legacy bare-SHA twin write's un-migrated `.tmp` shape is intentional (it predates
  the pid-suffix convention) or migrate it too for consistency.

## Acceptance Criteria

The count-stamp write path has an explicit test for its temp-file naming, and the legacy-write
inconsistency is either documented as intentional or fixed.

## Technical Approach

1. `grep -rn '\.tmp"' \| grep -rn "\.tmp\`"` across `plugin/` and `tests/` for any remaining
   reference to the bare (non-pid-suffixed) `.tmp` shape tied to `verify/stamp.js`'s writes
   specifically (a broader repo-wide `.tmp` grep will also hit unrelated call sites — scope the
   sweep to files this migration actually touched).
2. Add a test in `tests/bin-lib/verify/stamp.test.js`, mirroring the existing pid-suffix test at
   line 60 but targeting the count-stamp write (`verify.js:374`) instead of the JSON stamp write
   — same fake-fs assertion pattern (`!Object.keys(fsImpl.files).some((p) => p.endsWith('.tmp'))`
   plus a pid-suffix check on the actual tmp key used).
3. For the legacy bare-SHA twin write (`stamp.js:69`): read the surrounding comment ("The legacy
   bare-SHA twin write just below is untouched (Non-Goals) — independently transitional,
   unrelated to this migration's collision-safety concern") to judge whether leaving it
   unmigrated was a deliberate scoping decision from the original PR, and either add a comment
   confirming that's still the right call, or migrate it to the same `writeFileAtomic` primitive
   for consistency if no reason to keep it separate survives scrutiny.

### Key Files

- `plugin/bin/lib/verify/stamp.js` (lines ~63, ~69) — the migrated JSON-stamp write and the
  still-legacy bare-SHA twin write
- `plugin/bin/verify.js` (line 374) — the count-stamp write, needs test coverage
- `tests/bin-lib/verify/stamp.test.js` (~line 60) — add the count-stamp temp-filename test

  ("Non-Goals") — don't assume this is an oversight without reading that reasoning first; the

## Current State

Found during a pre-release whole-branch review of `tests/`. #2026's change to
`plugin/bin/verify.js` (confirmed, ~line 305: `const retryHook = async (result, ctx) => { if
(!decl) return result; ...`) replaced `flakyEnabled = Boolean(decl && decl.flaky.files.length >
0)` with `if (!decl) return result`, per that change's own comment: "an empty/absent `flaky`
declaration still needs a `retryDecision.reason` recorded." `declaration.js`'s `readDeclaration`
(confirmed, ~line 126: `let flaky = { files: [], maxRetries: DEFAULT_MAX_RETRIES };`) always
defaults `flaky = { files: [], ... }`, so the empty-allowlist case is the *only* new behavior
this change introduces.

`tests/bin-lib/verify/cli.test.js:1103` (`noParseArgs`, the only new test in this range,
confirmed present) declares `flaky: { files: ['tests/flaky.test.js'] }` — a non-empty allowlist.
No test in the file exercises an empty or absent `flaky` declaration, so the actual behavior
change this record shipped is untested — it passes identically before and after the fix.

## Deliverables

Add a test that supplies an empty or absent `flaky` declaration and asserts
`retryDecision.reason` is recorded as the change's comment describes.

The new test fails against a revert of #2026's `verify.js` change (proving it actually exercises
the behavior) and passes on the current code.

Add a new test case alongside the existing `noParseArgs`-based test at
`tests/bin-lib/verify/cli.test.js:1103`, using a declaration with either no `flaky` key at all,

Surface: infra

## Current State

`bin/materialize.js`'s `--multi-record-slug` handling (confirmed still present, lines ~306-308)
writes the spec under `path.join(opts.runDir, 'spec-' + opts.multiRecordSlug, 'work')` rather
than `path.join(opts.runDir, 'work')` — an existing test
(`tests/bin-lib/issues/materialize-format.test.js:297`, "materialize CLI: --multi-record-slug
writes under spec-{slug}/work/") documents this as the CLI's own intended contract: `--run-dir`
is expected to be the **parent** directory, and `--multi-record-slug` descends into a per-spec
`spec-{slug}/` subdirectory beneath it.

The reported failure is a **contract mismatch at the call site**, not necessarily a bug in the
CLI's own tested behavior: `flow/materialize.md`'s own documented CLI signature says flatly "the
CLI writes `{--run-dir}/work/{n}-spec.md` exactly under whatever path is passed" — it does not
mention `--multi-record-slug` at all, and does not say when a caller should or shouldn't pass it
during a multi-spec run. `flow/multi-spec.md` (line 113) documents `PIPELINE_RUN_DIR` as already
resolving to the per-spec `{parent}/spec-{N}/` subdirectory for a multi-spec run. The reporter's
repro shows a call site materializing the third record of a multi-spec run with
`--run-dir {parent}/spec-C` (already per-spec) **and** `--multi-record-slug A-B-C` together —
under the CLI's own tested contract, that double-supplies the per-spec descent: once via
`--run-dir` already being `spec-C`, and again via `--multi-record-slug` appending a second
`spec-A-B-C` level beneath it, producing
`{parent}/spec-C/spec-A-B-C/work/C-spec.md` instead of the expected
`{parent}/spec-C/work/C-spec.md`.

`opts.multiRecordSlug` has no other use in `materialize.js` besides this one workDir
construction — it carries no other side effect that a fix here would need to preserve.

## Deliverables

- Locate the exact call site (in `/flow`'s or `/build`'s multi-spec materialization sequence)
  that invokes `materialize.js` with both an already-per-spec `--run-dir` and
  `--multi-record-slug` set — determine whether that call site should stop passing
  `--multi-record-slug` (since `--run-dir` has already resolved to the per-spec directory), or
  whether it should instead pass the shared **parent** directory as `--run-dir` and let
  `--multi-record-slug` do the per-spec descent, matching the CLI's own currently-tested
  contract.
- Apply whichever fix resolves the mismatch without breaking the CLI's existing tested contract
  (`materialize-format.test.js:297`) for any caller that correctly relies on the parent+slug
  shape — update that test only if the CLI's contract itself is deliberately changed, with a
  clear reason recorded for the change.
- Update `flow/materialize.md`'s documented CLI signature to state explicitly when
  `--multi-record-slug` should (and should not) be passed alongside `--run-dir`, closing the gap
  that let this mismatch ship silently in the first place.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A multi-spec `/claude-tweaks:flow "#A,#B,#C"` run in `auto` mode with a shared worktree
  materializes each spec's file at `{parent}/spec-{N}/work/{n}-spec.md` — no extra
  `spec-{slug}` nesting level — matching the reporter's own stated expectation and what `/build`'s
  "read it in place" check, the consolidated console's `spec-{N}/work/{n}-spec.md` enumeration,
  and the archive's per-spec `git mv` all already assume.
- `materialize-format.test.js`'s existing `--multi-record-slug` test either still passes
  unchanged (if the fix is call-site-only) or is deliberately updated to reflect a changed CLI
  contract (if the fix changes `materialize.js` itself) — never left silently contradicting the
  new call-site behavior.
- `flow/materialize.md` states the `--run-dir`/`--multi-record-slug` interaction explicitly, so a
  future caller cannot reproduce this same double-nesting by accident.
- `npm test` passes.

## Technical Approach

Grep every call site invoking `materialize.js` with `--multi-record-slug` (already found:
`dispatch/task-prompt.md`'s prompt template — verify whether `/flow`'s own multi-spec sequence,
not just dispatch's fan-out template, has an equivalent invocation) and, for each, determine what
value it actually passes for `--run-dir` at that point in the sequence — a per-spec
`{parent}/spec-{N}` (per `flow/multi-spec.md:113`'s own `PIPELINE_RUN_DIR` documentation) or the
shared parent. The fix is whichever of these restores a single level of per-spec nesting:
(a) stop passing `--multi-record-slug` when `--run-dir` already resolved to the per-spec
directory, or (b) pass the parent directory as `--run-dir` and let `--multi-record-slug` do the
descent, matching the CLI's own currently-tested contract. Prefer (a) unless there's a concrete
reason the call site needs the parent path for something else at that same call — changing the
call site is lower blast radius than changing the CLI's own tested contract, since the CLI's
`spec-{slug}` shape may have other current callers this record hasn't traced.

### Key Files

- The identified call site (in `/flow` or `/build`'s multi-spec materialization sequence, or
  `dispatch/task-prompt.md`'s prompt template — confirm which is actually implicated by the
  repro) — fix the `--run-dir`/`--multi-record-slug` argument pairing
- `plugin/bin/materialize.js` (~lines 306-308) — only touched if the CLI's own contract is
  deliberately changed instead of the call site
- `tests/bin-lib/issues/materialize-format.test.js` (~line 297) — update only if the CLI
  contract changes
- `plugin/skills/flow/materialize.md` — document the `--run-dir`/`--multi-record-slug`
  interaction explicitly

## Gotchas

- Do not fix this by simply deleting `--multi-record-slug`'s effect from `materialize.js` without
  checking `materialize-format.test.js:297` and every other call site first — that test currently
  documents the flag's nesting behavior as intentional CLI contract, not a leftover bug; changing
  it silently could break a caller this record hasn't traced.
- Windows path handling: the original report was filed on Windows 11 — verify the fix's path
  joining is platform-neutral (`path.join`, already in use, is fine; just don't introduce a
  hardcoded `/` anywhere while touching this code).

## Original request

**Summary:** With `--multi-record-slug`, `bin/materialize.js` writes the spec under `{run-dir}/spec-{N}/spec-{slug}/work/` instead of `{run-dir}/spec-{N}/work/`.

**Kind:** Defect

**Affected component:** bin/materialize.js (`--multi-record-slug`), flow/materialize.md

**Repro steps:**
1. Start a multi-spec `/claude-tweaks:flow "#A,#B,#C"` run in `auto` mode with a shared worktree (`worktree-always: true`), so the parent run dir holds `spec-A/`, `spec-B/`, `spec-C/`.
2. For the third record, materialize with `PIPELINE_RUN_DIR={parent}/spec-C` and `--multi-record-slug A-B-C`.
3. Look for `{parent}/spec-C/work/C-spec.md`.

**Expected vs. actual:**
Expected: the materialized file lands at `{PIPELINE_RUN_DIR}/work/{n}-spec.md` — the path `/build`'s "read it in place" check, the consolidated console's `spec-{N}/work/{n}-spec.md` release-claim enumeration and the archive's per-spec `git mv` all expect.
Actual: the multi-record slug is appended as a second `spec-` directory level beneath the per-spec run dir that `PIPELINE_RUN_DIR` already names: `{parent}/spec-C/spec-A-B-C/work/C-spec.md`. The file had to be moved by hand (one extra commit) before the build could adopt it.

Observed on plugin 6.114.1, Windows 11, a private project on a GHE remote.

**Definition:** Clear

**Plugin version:** 6.114.1

groups.body:
Surface: backend

## Overview

The Subagent Contract (`plugin/skills/_shared/subagent-output-contract.md`) currently requires
every dispatched subagent's reply to open with one of `DONE` / `DONE_WITH_CONCERNS` /
`NEEDS_CONTEXT` / `BLOCKED` as the literal first line. This has failed in production three
separate times (`#606`, `#1653`, `#1868`) despite explicit `WRONG:` examples at every dispatch
site — models reliably produce a clear concluding verdict but are unreliable at *opening* with one
before any reasoning. This unit is the keystone of a 5-unit decomposition (parent #2264): it moves
the canonical status signal to a labeled trailing line and makes the mechanical checker in
`plugin/bin/lib/hooks/subagent-stop.js` lenient about exact position. Every other unit in this
decomposition (WU2-WU5, each `Blocked by` this one) edits inline dispatch-prompt copies of the
same rule, and each of those edits must match the canonical text this unit establishes — so this
unit lands first.

**Complexity:** Medium
**Estimated tasks:** 5

## Non-Goals

- Changing `subagent-stop.js`'s best-effort, non-blocking posture — it remains a diagnostic log,
  never a gate. This migration adds no new enforcement mechanism.
- Retrofitting `plugin/skills/harness-health/judge-procedure.md` (~228) or
  `plugin/skills/harness-health/SKILL.md` (~69) — their entire reply *is* the status line
  ("reply with nothing but a single status line"), so the narration-creeps-in-before-it failure
  mode this migration targets cannot occur there. Left as a follow-up for a later record.
- Changing the four status words themselves, their routing meaning, or the Template A/B/C content
  that follows the status line.
- Editing any of the other 21 dispatch-site files that carry an inline copy of the old
  position-asserting instruction — those are WU2 through WU5 in this same decomposition, each
  `Blocked by` this unit.
- Hook-side reply rewriting (stripping narration before the check runs) — rejected in the design
  doc's Rationale: it silently edits the audit trail, so the logged reply no longer matches what
  the subagent actually said.

## Current State

- Canonical rule: `plugin/skills/_shared/subagent-output-contract.md` states or depends on the
  "first line" position requirement at approximately lines 80, 93, 256, 278, and 286 — including
  the Implementer Status Protocol table's framing sentence, the "Check the status word's position,
  not merely its presence" paragraph (which cites the `#606`/`#1653` incidents by name), and the
  fan-out dispatch-shape example block.
- Detection code: `plugin/bin/lib/hooks/subagent-stop.js` exports `STATUS_RE =
  /^(?:-\s+)?(?:\*\*Status:\*\*\s+)?(DONE|DONE_WITH_CONCERNS|NEEDS_CONTEXT|BLOCKED)\b/` and applies
  it to the first line of the last assistant turn only (`lastAssistantText`). The file's header
  comment documents this as an "E3: Subagent Contract status-line check (warn tier)" — best-effort,
  never blocking, with two documented false-positive sources already carved out (a dispatch
  declaring a different contract; an absent `agent_transcript_path`).
- Test coverage: zero. No `tests/hooks-subagent-stop*.test.js` file exists, and no existing test
  anywhere exercises `STATUS_RE`'s actual matching behavior — `contract-violation` appears in a
  handful of other test files only as an event-name string in unrelated contexts (dispatcher
  registration, friction-events consumption).

## Deliverables

- [ ] Rewrite `plugin/skills/_shared/subagent-output-contract.md`'s canonical status-line rule (all
      5 cited locations: ~80, ~93, ~256, ~278, ~286) so the reply's **last non-empty line** must
      read exactly `STATUS: DONE` (or `STATUS: DONE_WITH_CONCERNS` / `STATUS: NEEDS_CONTEXT` /
      `STATUS: BLOCKED`) — a labeled line, never a bare trailing word. Update the Implementer
      Status Protocol table's framing sentence and the "Check the status word's position" paragraph
      to describe the new trailing-line convention instead of the retired first-line one. For
      review-style agents (Template A), the trailing status line follows the findings table
      (reversing the current "status line, then table" order); for search/scout-style (B/C), the
      trailing status line follows whatever the template's own content is.
- [ ] Update the file's `WRONG:` examples (and the fan-out dispatch-shape example block) to show
      the *new* failure modes worth warning about — a bare trailing word instead of the labeled
      `STATUS:` line, and a status line that isn't truly the last non-empty line of the reply —
      rather than the retired first-line-narration example (`"Based on my review, DONE"`).
- [ ] Replace `subagent-stop.js`'s `STATUS_RE`-based first-line-only check with a two-tier
      canonical/lenient detection function: (1) canonical — does the last non-empty line match
      `^STATUS: (DONE|DONE_WITH_CONCERNS|NEEDS_CONTEXT|BLOCKED)$` exactly? Compliant, no event
      logged. (2) lenient fallback — does the bare status word appear as the first token of any of
      the first 3 lines, or the last 3 lines? Compliant, but log an informational
      `contract-violation` event variant noting the non-canonical position (distinguishable from a
      hard violation in the logged event's fields — see Data / API Surface below). (3) neither —
      genuine violation, log `contract-violation` exactly as today, unchanged behavior.
- [ ] Update `subagent-stop.js`'s header comment (currently documents the first-line contract and
      its two known false-positive sources) to describe the new two-tier detection shape.
- [ ] Create `tests/hooks-subagent-stop.test.js` (new file — no test currently exercises this
      hook's detection logic at all) covering all four cases in Acceptance Criteria below.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. `tests/hooks-subagent-stop.test.js` includes a canonical-format detection test: a reply whose
   last non-empty line is exactly `STATUS: DONE` (and separately, one for each of
   `DONE_WITH_CONCERNS`, `NEEDS_CONTEXT`, `BLOCKED`) is detected as compliant with no
   `contract-violation` event logged.
2. The same test file includes a lenient-fallback detection test: a reply whose status word
   appears as the first token of one of the first-or-last 3 lines (but not as the canonical
   trailing `STATUS:` line) is detected as compliant, AND the test asserts the informational
   log variant fires — not the hard-violation `contract-violation` event.
3. The same test file includes a genuine-violation detection test: a reply where the status word
   appears nowhere in the first-or-last 3 lines (or not at all) is detected as non-compliant and
   logs `contract-violation` exactly as today's behavior — unchanged from the pre-migration
   detection.
4. The same test file includes a migration-safety test proving the design doc's rollout-safety
   claim directly: an old-format reply (the bare status word as the literal first line, with no
   trailing `STATUS:` line anywhere in the reply) is STILL accepted as compliant by the new
   lenient fallback — this is what makes the format migration itself safe with no explicit
   transition period.
5. `plugin/skills/_shared/subagent-output-contract.md`'s `WRONG:` examples (all instances) show the
   new failure modes — a bare trailing word instead of the labeled `STATUS:` line, and a status
   line that isn't truly the last non-empty line — and no longer show the retired
   first-line-narration example as the primary illustration.
6. `npm test` passes with no regressions after all edits in this unit land.
7. The two-tier detection function excludes markdown table-row lines (lines starting with `|`
   after trimming) from the tier-2 lenient-fallback candidate window, with a test proving a
   findings-table row containing a matching word does not itself trigger a false
   lenient-compliant match when the reply's actual trailing status line is missing.

## Technical Approach

Exactly the design doc's Decision section (New canonical format + Checker leniency subsections) —
reproduced here since the design doc is deleted once this decomposition lands:

**New canonical format.** The reply's last non-empty line must read exactly `STATUS: {WORD}`. A
labeled line, not a bare trailing word, because a bare trailing word risks colliding with prose
that happens to end in a matching token ("...the tests are done" reads as ambiguous;
"...the tests are done\nSTATUS: DONE" does not). The label makes the line unambiguous and
trivially greppable: `grep -E '^STATUS: (DONE|DONE_WITH_CONCERNS|NEEDS_CONTEXT|BLOCKED)$'` against
the last non-empty line of a reply.

**Checker leniency (subsumes rollout safety).** `subagent-stop.js`'s detection changes from "does
the first line match `STATUS_RE`" to the three-tier check in Deliverables above. This single
fallback rule does double duty: it is the mechanical leniency that tolerates ordinary model drift
(the status word landing one line off from where the contract technically wants it), and it is
also what makes the format migration itself safe with no explicit transition period to manage — a
dispatch's full round-trip (prompt sent, subagent replies, reply checked) happens within one Task
call, using whichever plugin version is loaded when the *check* runs, not when the *prompt* was
sent. An in-flight dispatch given an old-format prompt (status word first) whose reply is checked
after this migration ships is still accepted by the lenient fallback's first-K-lines check.

### Data / API Surface

The informational log variant from Deliverable 3 must be distinguishable from a hard
`contract-violation` in the logged event's own fields (e.g. an added `variant: 'lenient'` /
`variant: 'canonical'` / absent-for-hard-violation field, or equivalent) — the design doc's own
wording is "log an informational `contract-violation` event variant... visible for someone to
notice a dispatch site is still using the old shape, but never a hard failure." Name the exact
field/shape chosen in this deliverable's own commit; downstream consumers of the friction-events
log (`bin/lib/hooks/friction-events` or equivalent) are out of this unit's scope to update, per
Non-Goals — a consumer keying on the `contract-violation` event name alone (with no `variant`
check) will keep treating the informational variant as a hard violation until it is separately
updated; this is an accepted, intentional boundary of this unit's scope, not an oversight.

### Detection Boundary Rules (resolved during Step 5 red-team review)

- **Tier-2 match shape.** The lenient fallback matches either the bare status word OR a labeled
  `STATUS: {WORD}` line (tier-1's own exact pattern, just off-position) as the first token of a
  candidate line — after stripping the same optional `- ` / `**Status:**` prefixes the existing
  `STATUS_RE` already strips. Either form landing in the candidate window is lenient-compliant.
- **Window counts non-empty lines only**, matching tier-1's own "last non-empty line" convention —
  blank lines never count toward the first-3/last-3 window, and the two windows may overlap for a
  short reply (≤6 non-empty lines total); checked as a union, not a strict partition.
- **Canonical exact-match is on the trimmed line** (trailing whitespace ignored) and is
  case-sensitive — `STATUS: done` does not match tier 1 (it may still match tier 2's bare-word
  check if `done` itself were a valid word, which it isn't, so an all-lowercase reply always falls
  through to genuine-violation, unchanged from today's case-sensitive behavior).
- **Table-row exclusion.** A candidate line that is a markdown table row (starts with `|` after
  trimming) is excluded from the tier-2 window — this prevents a Template A findings table's own
  cell content (which may itself contain a matching word) from producing a false lenient-compliant
  match when the reply's real trailing status line is missing or malformed.
- **Decorated variants are an accepted gap, not a blocking one.** A bolded canonical line (e.g.
  `**STATUS: DONE**`) matches neither tier 1 exactly nor the existing prefix carve-outs (which
  target a different contract's bold `**Status:**` bullet shape, not this new line) — left
  unhandled by design, consistent with the checker's best-effort, non-blocking posture.
- The two existing false-positive carve-outs (a dispatch declaring a different contract; an absent
  `agent_transcript_path`) and `isExemptAgentType` are unaffected and still evaluated before either
  detection tier runs.
- **Template B/C placement.** The trailing status line is the reply's absolute last non-empty line,
  after all of that template's own required content — identical to every other site's rule, just
  with no findings table to follow it.

### Key Files

- `plugin/skills/_shared/subagent-output-contract.md` — canonical rule text at ~80, ~93, ~256,
  ~278, ~286; `WRONG:` examples and the fan-out dispatch-shape example block.
- `plugin/bin/lib/hooks/subagent-stop.js` — replace `STATUS_RE`'s first-line-only check with the
  two-tier canonical/lenient detection function; update the header comment.
- `tests/hooks-subagent-stop.test.js` — new file, zero prior coverage of this hook's detection
  logic.

## Gotchas

- **Related:** #2036 — "SubagentStop hook misattributes contract-violation to main-session
  narration." Cross-link only, not a dependency: #2036 is a genuinely separate bug (the hook reads
  the wrong transcript source, attributing a violation to main-session narration instead of the
  actual subagent reply) in the same function this unit touches. Do not fold #2036's proposed
  exemption into this unit's scope — leave its own resolution to its own record.
- `STATUS_RE` already carries two documented false-positive carve-outs (a dispatch declaring a
  different contract shape, e.g. `superpowers:subagent-driven-development`'s bold `**Status:**`
  bullet; an absent `agent_transcript_path`) — preserve both when rewriting the detection function,
  they are orthogonal to the position-leniency change this unit makes.
- `isExemptAgentType` (third-party plugin agent exemption, `#1596`) is untouched by this migration
  — it gates whether the check runs at all, not how the status line is located within a reply that
  does get checked.
- The two structurally-immune harness-health files (Non-Goals above) already comply with the *old*
  first-line rule by construction ("nothing but a single status line") and will also comply with
  the *new* trailing-line rule by the same construction (their one line is simultaneously first and
  last) — no migration risk there, which is exactly why they're a low-priority follow-up rather
  than in-scope here.
- Keep `subagent-stop.js`'s best-effort, non-blocking posture completely unchanged — this is a
  detection-shape change only, never a new gate.
- **Accepted duplication tradeoff (raised in Step 5 red-team).** This decomposition's other 4
  units (WU2-WU5) each carry their own inline dispatch-prompt copy of the same canonical rule
  rather than a single centralized reference — consistent with how every dispatch site in this
  plugin already works today (agents only see their own prompt; a shared-file reference would not
  reach them, per the Subagent Contract's own "Letting agents read sibling files" anti-pattern).
  Centralizing the canonical *text* into one file the *human maintainer* edits once (as opposed to
  what each dispatched *agent* sees) is a real architectural question worth its own record, but is
  out of scope for a status-line migration and not required for this unit's acceptance.

## Manual Steps

None — every deliverable has a direct CLI/code path (file edits, a new test file, `npm test`).

groups.body:
Surface: infra

## Current State
`bin/lib/verify/flaky.js`'s `planRetry` builds `new Set(flaky.files)` and treats a failing file as allowlisted only when `listed.has(file)` — exact string equality against the declaration's `flaky.files` entries. The same `verify-scope.json` file's `rules[].match` entries are globs, compiled by `bin/lib/issues/blast-radius.js`'s `globToRegExp` (memoized, `**` spans segments, `*` stays segment-bound, every other character escaped) and applied in `scope.js`. So one schema carries two matching semantics: a project can write `tests/**` in a rule but must enumerate `tests/flaky/a.test.js`, `tests/flaky/b.test.js`, … in the allowlist and edit the list every time a flaky file is added. `declaration.js` validates `flaky.files` only as "an array of path strings", and `test/verification.md`'s Flake handling paragraph documents the entries as "exact repo-relative paths" that "must match the failing-file paths exactly as the suite's own output prints them".

## Deliverables
- [ ] `planRetry` matches each failing file against `flaky.files` with `globToRegExp(entry).test(file)` (any entry matching allowlists the file), keeping the `unlisted: [...]` reason and the fail-safe on any unmatched file; an entry with no glob metacharacter compiles to an anchored literal, so existing exact-path lists behave byte-for-byte as today.
- [ ] `declaration.js`'s `flaky.files` validation message reads "an array of path or glob strings"; no schema change.
- [ ] `test/verification.md`'s Flake handling paragraph: "exact repo-relative paths" becomes "repo-relative paths or globs (the same `**`/`*` forms `rules[].match` accepts)", and the sentence that entries must match the suite's printed paths keeps its warning about package-relative output — a glob is matched against the same printed path.
- [ ] Tests in `tests/bin-lib/verify/flaky.test.js`: a `tests/flaky/**` entry allowlists a new file under that directory; an exact entry still matches only itself; `tests/*.test.js` does not match a nested file (segment-bound `*`); an entry that matches nothing leaves the unlisted reason naming the file. `tests/bin-lib/verify/declaration.test.js` gets the message text update if it pins the old wording.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Existing exact-path `flaky.files` entries produce the same `planRetry` decisions as before (the existing flaky cases pass unmodified).
2. A glob entry allowlists every failing file it matches, with `**` and `*` behaving exactly as they do for `rules[].match`.
3. A failing file matched by no entry still blocks the retry with `unlisted:` naming it.
4. The `flakyHits` counter and the `flaky-allowlist` escalation CAVEAT stay keyed by the concrete file path, never by the glob; `npm test` is green.

## Technical Approach
Reuse the engine the file already shares a schema with: `scope.js` imports `globToRegExp` from `bin/lib/issues/blast-radius.js`; `flaky.js` imports the same function and replaces the `Set` lookup with a `some(entry => globToRegExp(entry).test(file))` pass. The regex builder escapes every non-glob character, so backward compatibility for exact paths is a property of the compiler, not a special case. The retry command template still substitutes the concrete file, so nothing downstream sees a glob.

### Key Files
- `plugin/bin/lib/verify/flaky.js` — `planRetry` (the `listed` Set and `unlisted` filter).
- `plugin/bin/lib/issues/blast-radius.js` — `globToRegExp` (read-only, imported).
- `plugin/bin/lib/verify/declaration.js` — `flaky.files` validation message.
- `plugin/skills/test/verification.md` — Flake handling paragraph.
- `tests/bin-lib/verify/flaky.test.js`, `tests/bin-lib/verify/declaration.test.js`.

## Gotchas
- `globToRegExp` has no `?` wildcard (it escapes `?`); say "the same forms `rules[].match` accepts" rather than promising full glob syntax.
- The escalation counter is what tells a maintainer which concrete file keeps flaking; a glob allowlist must not blur that, so the per-file `flakyHits` key is unchanged and the `flaky-allowlist` CAVEAT still names the file.
- `/claude-tweaks:wrap-up`'s leftover routing files an escalation as a backlog record per file; a glob entry does not change that shape.

## Original request
Found by the pre-v6.119.0 whole-branch review (range e7d6d9331..4db32e020).

groups.body:
Surface: infra

## Current State

`plugin/skills/test/verification.md`'s "Flake handling (tests check only)" section makes the runner the owner of listed-flaky retries (#1925) and keeps one agent-performed isolation step for a failure in an **unlisted** file: re-run that one file (`node --test path/to/file.test.js`), isolated pass → flake, isolated fail → regression. That step presupposes a file name. `bin/lib/verify/flaky.js`'s `planRetry` returns `{ retry: false, reason: 'no-parse' }` when `extractFailingFiles` yields nothing (`sniffFamily` classified the output as `generic`, or the family's failing-file pattern did not match), and `bin/verify.js` records that decision without acting on it; the prose has no branch for it, so a `no-parse` failure is presented as a flat regression with no flake adjudication. Before #1925, the isolate-and-rerun-once rule was unconditional.

"Isolating pre-existing failures by file, not by keyword grep" (the section above the flake handling) is the other half of the same rule and likewise assumes extractable paths. `report.json`'s check entry already carries the retry decision as `retryDecision` (`{ retry: false, reason: 'no-parse' | 'unlisted: […]' | 'no-template' | 'max-retries-0' | 'unreadable-log' }`, written by `verify.js` and carried by `report.js`), so the signal the prose needs exists; nothing in the prose or the stdout summary reads it.

## Deliverables

- [ ] **Two named isolation paths.** `verification.md`'s Flake handling section states them explicitly: **named-file isolation** (today's unlisted-file rule, unchanged) and **whole-suite re-run** for a `no-parse` failure: re-run the `tests` check once through the runner (`node "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/bin/verify.js" --cmd tests="{command}"` with the same scope and `--no-stamp`-equivalent posture so a second pass never records a pass stamp on its own), then adjudicate: second run passes → **flake** (reported exactly as the named-file flake is, verdict unchanged); fails again → **regression**. One re-run, never more; the whole-suite cost is stated as the reason this path is the fallback, not the default.
- [ ] **The prose and the summary read the existing decision.** `verification.md` tells the agent to read `retryDecision.reason` from `report.json` (`no-parse` → whole-suite path; an `unlisted:` reason → named-file path) instead of re-deriving the extractor's outcome; `bin/verify.js`'s stdout summary for a failed `tests` check gains the clause `(retry: no-parse — whole-suite re-run applies)` so the path is visible without opening the report.
- [ ] **Pre-existing-failures section cross-reference.** "Isolating pre-existing failures by file" gains one sentence pointing at the whole-suite path for output with no extractable paths, so the two sections agree.
- [ ] **Tests.** `tests/bin-lib/verify/cli.test.js`: stdout carries the no-parse clause for a generic-family failing fixture and no clause for a passing check; the existing `retryDecision` report cases stay unchanged. A prose pin (sized like `tests/verify-scope-declaration.test.js`) asserting the two path names and the one-re-run cap in `verification.md`.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. `verification.md` names both isolation paths, the `no-parse` trigger, the single whole-suite re-run, and the flake/regression adjudication for it; the named-file paragraph is byte-identical to today apart from the new heading.
2. `verification.md` names `retryDecision.reason` as the selector between the two paths; the stdout summary shows the no-parse clause for a `no-parse` failure and nothing for a passing check.
3. A generic-family failing fixture run through `verify.js` twice, with the second run passing, is adjudicated as a flake by the documented procedure and never records a pass stamp from the re-run alone.
4. `npm test` green; existing `tests/bin-lib/verify/*` cases pass with only additive assertions.

## Technical Approach

Restore the old rule's universality without losing #1925's precision: keep named-file isolation as the cheap first path and add the whole-suite re-run only where no file can be named. Read the runner's existing `retryDecision` rather than adding new detection, so the prose and the report agree on which path is in force. Do not add a runner-owned whole-suite retry: a full-suite re-run is minutes of work the agent should choose consciously, per the section's own cost note.

### Key Files

- `plugin/skills/test/verification.md` — Flake handling: two named paths; pre-existing-failures cross-reference
- `plugin/bin/verify.js` — stdout summary clause for a `no-parse` retry decision
- `tests/bin-lib/verify/cli.test.js`, a prose-pin sibling of `tests/verify-scope-declaration.test.js` — new cases

## Gotchas

- The re-run must not write a pass stamp by itself (`stamp.js`'s dirty-tree rule and #1921's stamp semantics stay authoritative); the adjudication is the agent's, the stamp is the runner's.
- `looksPassing` and `extractFailingFiles` are separate: a `no-parse` decision can coexist with a clearly failing exit code, which is exactly the case this record covers. The retry path already strips ANSI before extracting (`verify.js`), so colour alone does not produce `no-parse`; an unknown runner format does.
- `#1837` (shaped in this sweep) adds a vitest dialect and ANSI stripping; once it lands, fewer failures are `no-parse`, but the path still exists for unknown runners.
- Keep the one-re-run cap in prose and in the pin; an unbounded re-run loop is the failure this rule exists to prevent.

## Original request

## Current State
`plugin/skills/test/verification.md` line 151's mandatory isolate-and-rerun-once rule is scoped only to a failure `extractFailingFiles` can name a file for (an "unlisted file" case). A `no-parse` failure (`sniffFamily` returns `generic`, or the extractor can't match the runner's output format) has no isolation procedure at all — it's reported as a flat regression with no flake adjudication, unlike the old universal rule that applied regardless of whether a file could be named.

## Deliverables
- [ ] Extend `verification.md`'s isolate-and-rerun-once procedure to cover the `no-parse` case — e.g. re-running the full suite once (since no single file can be named) before treating a failure as a confirmed regression.
- [ ] Document the distinction between "named-file isolation" and "whole-suite re-run" as the two isolation paths, so a reader can tell which applies.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. `verification.md`'s isolation rule explicitly covers both the named-file and no-parse cases.
2. No change to the named-file path's existing behavior.

## Original request
Found by the pre-v6.119.0 whole-branch review (range e7d6d9331..4db32e020): the isolate-and-rerun-once rule regressed from unconditional to named-file-only when #1925's extractor-driven isolation replaced the old universal recipe.

Origin: brainstorm on #1904 (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-05-pipeline-ceremony-cost-design.md, "Filed separately")
Defer-reason: genuinely-larger

**Related:** #1987

## Current State

A `/claude-tweaks:flow` second call (`review,polish,wrap-up`) loads several hundred KB of skill prose before doing any work: `plugin/skills/_shared/` is 1.3 MB, `wrap-up/` alone is 408 KB, `flow/` 348 KB, and each 40 KB file is roughly 10k tokens. Reading the operative files shows that roughly half of most of them is provenance rather than procedure: which record moved a paragraph ("extracted for #887", "split out per #635"), which commit deleted a design doc ("deleted `70849915`"), and retold incident narratives that `docs/incident-log.md` already holds under their `[IL-nn]` tag. The context-cost test (`bin/lib/skill-audit/tests/context-cost.test.js`) caps bytes per file but nothing measures bytes loaded per pipeline step, so the procedure-vs-provenance ratio is invisible. #1765 (fast-lane digest) addresses the same waste for the fast-lane path only; this record is the general case. Tokens, not minutes: prose loading costs money and context headroom (compaction pressure), not wall-clock.

This record is Phase 5 of #1987 (Skill context composer — per-run bundles composed by resolved condition, not per-file ceilings): #1987's Phases 1-4 ship the composer mechanism and its per-step measurement; this record consumes that measurement and does the prose-diet and scaffolding-dedupe pass on top of it.

## Deliverables

- [ ] A stated authoring rule in `docs/skill-authoring.md`: operative text (`## Step N` bodies, gate tables, Next Actions) states the rule and cites the `[IL-nn]` tag or record number; the narrative of why lives in `docs/incident-log.md` or `docs/decisions/`, never restated inline. One sentence of rationale per rule is allowed; a paragraph is not.
- [ ] Per-step composed-bytes measurement is delivered by #1990 (Per-step composed-bytes measurement in context-cost.js) — this record consumes that measurement, not builds it.
- [ ] A first trimming pass over the five pipeline skills plus the `_shared` files they cite, moving provenance out per the rule, with the conformance tests that pin the moved prose updated in the same change (the real cost of this record — every trim moves pins).
- [ ] Before/after bytes per step recorded in the PR description.
- [ ] Inject the Interaction-style directive once from the `SessionStart` hook (`plugin/bin/lib/hooks/session-start.js`) and delete the 35 verbatim copies (501 B each) from every SKILL.md, with the conformance tests that pin that paragraph retargeted to the hook output.
- [ ] Audit the per-skill `## Input`/`## Anti-Patterns`/`## Component-Skill Contract`/`## Next Actions` scaffolding (~260 KB of the 888 KB SKILL.md payload) with `bloat.js`'s existing provenance signals and trim author-facing narration.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `docs/skill-authoring.md` carries the rule and `harness-health` reports loaded bytes per pipeline step.
- [ ] The five pipeline skills' default-path loaded bytes drop by at least 25% with no change to which steps execute, verified by the existing conformance suites passing after pin updates.
- [ ] No `[IL-nn]` narrative is lost: every trimmed retelling still resolves to its incident-log entry by tag.

## Technical Approach

### Key Files

- `docs/skill-authoring.md`
- `plugin/bin/lib/skill-audit/`
- `plugin/skills/flow/SKILL.md`, `plugin/skills/flow/steps-and-gates.md`
- `plugin/skills/build/SKILL.md`

- `plugin/bin/lib/hooks/session-start.js`
- `plugin/bin/lib/skill-audit/bloat.js`
- `tests/` (prose conformance suites pinning the trimmed text)

Surface: infra

## Current State
`_shared/label-bootstrap.md`'s check-then-create loop creates every canonical label with `gh label create "$NAME" --description "$DESCRIPTION"` and no `--color`, so GitHub assigns each one a random palette color at creation. `bin/lib/issues/labels.js`'s `ensureLabelPayload(name, description)` validates only the description cap; the `LABELS_JSON` arrays every consumer substitutes are `[name, description]` pairs with no color slot. On this repo the result is arbitrary and in places inverted: `risk:low` is red-orange (`D93F0B`) while `risk:high` is blue (`0052CC`); `size:low` and `size:medium` share `E99695`; `priority:low` is purple and `priority:medium` blue. Nothing reads the colors today (the State-of-the-Union dashboard colors these dimensions on its own side), so the cost is human: a label list that cannot be scanned by color, and an API color that would be noise if any consumer started reading it.

The bootstrap's version marker (`claude-tweaks:bootstrapped-v6`) only triggers the create-if-missing loop after a bump; an existing label's color is never touched, so a color convention needs an explicit edit path for repos that already carry the set.

## Deliverables
- [ ] `LABELS_JSON` entries become `[name, description, color]` triples; `ensureLabelPayload(name, description, color)` validates `color` as six hex digits (uppercase-normalized) and rejects a missing or malformed one at construction, the same fail-loud posture the description cap has. The canonical array in `_shared/label-bootstrap.md`'s "Canonical LABELS_JSON — the full work-record taxonomy" section carries the colors.
- [ ] A color convention stated once in `_shared/work-record.md`'s label-family table (the taxonomy home) and applied in `label-bootstrap.md`'s array: severity dimensions grade red → amber → green (`risk:high` `D93F0B`, `risk:medium` `FBCA04`, `risk:low` `0E8A16`; `priority:high` `B60205`, `priority:medium` `FBCA04`, `priority:low` `C2E0C6`); `size:*` grades on one neutral hue by lightness (`size:high` `5319E7`, `size:medium` `8B5CF6`, `size:low` `D4C5F9`); `type:*` reuses GitHub's defaults (`type:bug` `D73A4A`, `type:feature` `A2EEEF`, `type:task` `EDEDED`); `auto:*` one hue, `bot:*` one hue, `needs:*` one hue, `ceremony:*` one hue — each family visually distinct from the graded dimensions.
- [ ] `label-bootstrap.md`'s loop passes `--color "$COLOR"` on create, and gains a reconcile branch on the version-bump path (`SKIP_BOOTSTRAP=false`): for each canonical label that already exists, `gh label edit "$NAME" --color "$COLOR" --description "$DESCRIPTION"` when either differs from the payload, so an existing repo converges to the convention on its next bootstrap; `LABEL_BOOTSTRAP_VERSION` bumps to `7`.
- [ ] Every consumer that substitutes its own `LABELS_JSON` subset (the six files citing `label-bootstrap.md`) is updated to triples, taking colors from the canonical array; `bin/lib/issue-branch-tracking.js`'s standalone `gh label create … --color FBCA04` line is left as is (it is not a canonical label) but noted.
- [ ] Tests: `tests/bin-lib/issues/labels.test.js` covers the color validation (valid, lowercase-normalized, missing, malformed); a conformance test asserts every canonical `LABELS_JSON` entry in `_shared/label-bootstrap.md` is a triple with a valid color and that graded dimensions follow the stated order; `tests/session-tmp-root-migration.test.js` and the other suites that scan `label-bootstrap.md`'s snippet stay green.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. A virgin repo bootstrapped by any consumer ends with every canonical label carrying its convention color; `gh label list --json name,color` on it matches the array.
2. On this repo, one bootstrap under version 7 rewrites `risk:*`, `priority:*`, and `size:*` to the convention without recreating labels or losing their descriptions or issue attachments.
3. `ensureLabelPayload` rejects a pair (no color) and a malformed color before any `gh` call.
4. The convention is written in exactly one place (`_shared/work-record.md`'s family table) with the values in exactly one array (`_shared/label-bootstrap.md`), and the conformance test pins both; `npm test` is green.

## Technical Approach
Extend the existing payload contract rather than adding a second color-only pass: the loop already carries name and description per label, and `gh label create`/`gh label edit` both accept `--color`, so a third array element is the smallest change that reaches every consumer through the one snippet they all cite. The reconcile branch is scoped to the version-bump path so the common `SKIP_BOOTSTRAP=true` case stays at zero `gh` calls (IL-85's cost). GitHub's own default palette is reused where a label maps to a default (bug/enhancement), and the graded dimensions use its well-known red/amber/green triplet so the meaning reads without a legend.

### Key Files
- `plugin/skills/_shared/label-bootstrap.md` — the loop, the marker version literal, the reconcile branch, the canonical `LABELS_JSON` section.
- `plugin/skills/_shared/work-record.md` — taxonomy home; the label-family table gains the convention column.
- `plugin/bin/lib/issues/labels.js` — `ensureLabelPayload`.
- `plugin/skills/capture/SKILL.md`, `plugin/skills/demo/SKILL.md`, `plugin/skills/init/bootstrap/step-17-work-record-backend.md`, `plugin/skills/wrap-up/cleanup-procedures-execution.md`, `plugin/skills/wrap-up/docs-health-integration.md`, `plugin/skills/wrap-up/verification-brief-parent-gate.md` — consumers substituting their own arrays.
- `tests/bin-lib/issues/labels.test.js`; the conformance suite for the taxonomy.

## Gotchas
- `gh label create --color` takes hex without `#`; keep the array values bare and let the conformance test reject a leading `#`.
- The reconcile branch must compare before editing: an unconditional `gh label edit` per label on every bump costs one API call per label per repo, which the marker exists to avoid; edit only on mismatch.
- The `claude-tweaks:bootstrapped-v{N}` marker label itself gets a fixed neutral color so it is visibly bookkeeping.
- Under `work-backend: local-files` there are no GitHub labels; the color is inert there and `ensureLabelPayload` still requires it so the array stays one shape.

## Original request

Right now `risk:*`, `priority:*`, and `size:*` labels (and similar dimension labels) don't appear to have a deliberate color convention set on GitHub — they likely render with default/arbitrary colors. Worth setting real colors that carry meaning (e.g. `risk:high` red, `risk:low` green, `priority:high` amber), the way GitHub's own default label set does for bug/enhancement/etc.

Context: the State-of-the-Union dashboard is adding semantic coloring for these dimensions on its own side (not pulling from GitHub's label colors yet), but if it ever does read real label colors from the API, having a real convention here means that data becomes meaningful instead of noise.
